name: Spleen
func: A fist-sized organ in the upper left abdomen that filters the blood. It removes old or damaged red blood cells, stores some blood cells and platelets, and fights germs in the blood, especially encapsulated bacteria.

levels.kid:
The **spleen** is a soft, purple organ about the size of your **fist**. It hides on the upper **left** side of your tummy, tucked behind your ribs.

It is like a **filter** and a **recycling center** for your blood. Red blood cells carry air around your body, but after about four months they get old and tired. The spleen catches the old ones and breaks them down so your body can reuse their parts, like the iron.

The spleen also has tiny **germ-fighting** cells that grab bad germs floating in your blood and help keep you from getting sick.
levels.hs:
The **spleen** is the largest organ of the **lymphatic system**. It is about 12 cm long and sits in the **left upper quadrant** of the abdomen, under the diaphragm and protected by the **9th to 11th ribs**. It touches the **stomach** in front, the **left kidney** behind and below, the **splenic flexure of the colon** below, and the **tail of the pancreas** at its hilum. Normally you cannot feel it in an exam.

Inside, the spleen has two kinds of tissue:
- **Red pulp**: a spongy network full of blood that **filters red blood cells**. Old, stiff or damaged cells get stuck and are eaten by **macrophages**, which recycle their iron.
- **White pulp**: clusters of **lymphocytes** around small arteries that **detect germs** in the blood and make **antibodies**.

The spleen also stores some **platelets** (about a third of them) and **monocytes**, ready to release when needed.

Because it is soft and full of blood, a hit to the left side, like in a sports or car accident, can **rupture** it and cause dangerous internal bleeding. People can live without a spleen, but they become more vulnerable to some serious infections.
levels.college:
The spleen is an **intraperitoneal** organ, held in place by peritoneal folds: the **gastrosplenic ligament** (carrying the short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels) and the **splenorenal ligament** (carrying the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas). Its **diaphragmatic surface** is smooth and convex; its **visceral surface** shows gastric, renal and colic impressions. Its long axis lies along the **10th rib**.

**Blood supply**: the **splenic artery**, a tortuous branch of the **celiac trunk**, runs along the upper border of the pancreas and divides into segmental branches at the hilum. The spleen has relatively few anastomoses between segments, so blocked branches cause wedge-shaped **infarcts**. The **splenic vein** runs behind the pancreas and joins the **superior mesenteric vein** to form the **portal vein**.

**Microanatomy**: central arterioles are sheathed by **periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS)**, rich in **T cells**, and B-cell **follicles**. At the edge of the white pulp lies the **marginal zone**, with specialized macrophages and **marginal zone B cells** that respond quickly to **polysaccharide capsules** of bacteria. Most blood then flows into the red pulp in an "**open**" circulation: cells leave the vessels into the **splenic cords (of Billroth)** and must squeeze back through narrow slits in the walls of the **venous sinusoids**. Healthy, flexible red cells pass; stiff, old or abnormal ones are trapped and destroyed.

**Accessory spleens** (splenunculi) occur in about 10–30% of people, most often near the hilum.
levels.phd:
The red pulp is a mechanical and biochemical test of red cells. Interendothelial slits in the sinusoids are only about 1–2 μm wide, so a red cell, roughly 7–8 μm across, must deform to pass. This screen removes cells with reduced deformability, abnormal shape (spherocytes, sickled cells) or rigid inclusions. Macrophages also perform **pitting**, removing inclusions such as **Howell–Jolly bodies** (nuclear remnants) and **Heinz bodies** while sending the repaired cell back into circulation. Ageing red cells are recognized by signals such as **phosphatidylserine** exposure, band 3 clustering with bound antibodies and loss of the "don't eat me" signal **CD47**.

Iron recycling is central: red pulp macrophages (which depend on the transcription factor **SPI-C**) break down heme with **heme oxygenase-1** and export iron through **ferroportin**, which is regulated by the liver hormone **hepcidin**. In inflammation, hepcidin rises and iron becomes trapped in macrophages, contributing to the **anemia of inflammation**.

The **marginal zone** captures blood-borne antigens. **Marginal zone B cells** make rapid, T-independent **IgM** responses against polysaccharide capsules, which explains the danger of encapsulated bacteria (*Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* type b, *Neisseria meningitidis*) after splenectomy. **Metallophilic** and **marginal zone macrophages** (with receptors like SIGN-R1 and MARCO) trap particles.

The spleen is also a **monocyte reservoir**: after a heart attack, splenic monocytes are mobilized in large numbers to the injured heart (shown by Swirski and Nahrendorf). In the embryo the spleen briefly helps make blood cells, and **extramedullary hematopoiesis** can return in disorders where the bone marrow fails.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: an enlarged spleen is felt below the **left costal margin**, moving down with inspiration toward the **right iliac fossa**, with a notch on its front edge, and you cannot get above it. Percussion over Traube's space can help.

**Splenomegaly** causes include infection (**infectious mononucleosis**, malaria), **portal hypertension** (cirrhosis), hemolytic anemias (hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia), and blood cancers (lymphoma, **chronic myeloid leukemia** and **myelofibrosis**, which can cause massive splenomegaly). **Hypersplenism** traps blood cells, lowering platelet and white cell counts. Contact sports are avoided during mononucleosis because an enlarged spleen ruptures more easily.

**Splenic trauma** is the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma. Signs include left upper quadrant pain, shock and **Kehr sign** (left shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation, via the phrenic nerve). Diagnosis: **FAST** ultrasound and **contrast CT**, graded by the **AAST** scale. Stable patients, especially children, are often managed **non-operatively** or with **splenic artery embolization**; unstable patients need surgery.

**Splenectomy** is also used for some cases of **immune thrombocytopenia** and hereditary spherocytosis. Afterward, patients face lifelong risk of **overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)** from encapsulated bacteria, so they receive **vaccines** (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) and education about urgent treatment for fever. A blood film after splenectomy shows **Howell–Jolly bodies** and target cells.

In **sickle cell disease**, repeated infarcts shrink the spleen (**autosplenectomy**), and young children can have life-threatening **splenic sequestration crises**.

keyPoints: Left upper quadrant behind ribs 9–11; touches stomach, left kidney, colon and pancreatic tail
Red pulp filters old red cells; white pulp mounts immune responses
Splenic artery from the celiac trunk; splenic vein joins the SMV to form the portal vein
Most commonly injured solid organ in blunt trauma; Kehr sign = left shoulder pain
Without a spleen: risk from encapsulated bacteria, so vaccinate

test.q: The splenic artery is a branch of the:
test.explain: The celiac trunk gives the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries.

test.q: Left shoulder tip pain after splenic rupture is called ______ sign.
test.explain: Blood irritates the diaphragm; pain is referred through the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) to the shoulder.

test.q: Which part of the spleen removes old and damaged red blood cells?
test.explain: Stiff or damaged red cells are trapped in the red pulp cords and eaten by macrophages.

test.q: After splenectomy, patients are at greatest risk from infection by:
test.explain: Marginal zone B cells and splenic macrophages are key defenses against encapsulated bacteria.

test.q: Nuclear remnants in red cells seen after splenectomy are ______ bodies.
test.explain: Normally the spleen 'pits' these out; without it they stay visible on a blood film.
